**MEMORANDUM**

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 6, 2026
**Re:** Vaigaind Data Halls, LLC / Trugeith Thermal Systems, Inc.: Review of Hall C Liquid-Cooling Deal Documents
**Privileged & Confidential: Attorney Work Product**

---

## 1. Summary

I reviewed all five documents in the folder:

- the Supply Agreement dated March 2, 2026 (the "**Agreement**");
- Statement of Work No. 2 dated August 24, 2026 (the "**SOW**");
- the Service Level Schedule (the "**SLS**");
- the Data Processing Addendum (the "**DPA**"); and
- the October–November 2026 freight and rigging email thread.

The commercial deal is a single-hall project. The Agreement defines the Project Site as Hall C at Secaucus (Agreement Recital B), and SOW No. 2 covers only the west half of Hall C. Four provisions, read together, put Vaigaind in a materially worse position than that deal implies.

| # | Priority | Issue | Location |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **HIGH** | Exclusivity reaches every Vaigaind and Affiliate facility in the US and Canada | SOW §2; Agreement §§1.1(d), 3.1 |
| 2 | **HIGH (time-sensitive)** | Phase 1 rejection notice was late, so Trugeith claims deemed acceptance | SOW Recital C; Agreement §7.3 |
| 3 | **HIGH** | DPA brings data-security and Security Incident liability back under the 12-month-fees cap | DPA §8.2; Agreement §§1.4, 12.2, 12.3(b) |
| 4 | **MEDIUM-HIGH** | Automatic five-year renewals with a narrow, early opt-out window | Agreement §2.2 |
| 5 | MEDIUM | Phase 2 rejection window will close before Phase 2 commissioning | SOW §§5.1, 8.4; Agreement §7.3 |
| 6 | LOW | Secondary points and the freight/rigging thread | Various |

**Practical point on leverage.** The signature blocks in every document in the folder are blank. The email thread shows the parties performing under SOW No. 2: M1 submittals were approved September 25, and Phase 2 delivery is set for January 18, 2027. We therefore need to confirm what has actually been signed (see Section 4).

The goal is to fix Issues 1, 3 and 4 in a single amendment, and to resolve Issue 2, before Phase 2 Products are delivered and invoiced. That invoice is about $4.19M for products under SOW §7.2. Trugeith wants the Phase 2 revenue, so this is the window in which we have leverage.

Any amendment must:

- be in writing and signed by both parties (Agreement §19.3); and
- to the extent it is done in an SOW, expressly identify the Agreement Sections amended and be signed by an authorized officer of each party (Agreement §1.2).

---

## 2. Issues, Analysis and Recommended Fixes

### Issue 1: Overbroad exclusivity (HIGH)

**Where:**
- SOW No. 2, Section 2 (Covered Sites)
- Agreement §1.1(d) (Covered Sites "has the meaning given in the applicable SOW")
- Agreement §3.1 (Exclusive Purchasing)

**What it says:**
- Agreement §3.1 requires Vaigaind, during the Term, to buy "all of its requirements for Covered Products for all Covered Sites exclusively from Supplier." It also bars Vaigaind from soliciting, purchasing or installing third-party Covered Products at any Covered Site.
- The Agreement does not define Covered Sites itself. It delegates the definition to the SOW.
- SOW §2 defines Covered Sites as "all data center facilities owned, leased or operated by Customer or any of its Affiliates in the United States and Canada, including the Project Site."
- "Covered Products" (Agreement §1.1(c)) covers CDUs, rear-door heat exchangers and any other liquid-cooling equipment of a type identified as a Product in any SOW. In practice, that is Vaigaind's entire liquid-cooling equipment category.

**Why the precedence clause does not help:** One might argue the Agreement body (§1.4, second) prevails over the SOW (fourth). That argument is weak.

- §1.4 resolves *conflicts*. Here the Agreement expressly hands the definition to the SOW, so there is no conflict to resolve.
- SOW §1.1 states that the SOW "does not amend any Section of the Agreement." Trugeith will say it fills in a definition the Agreement left open, which is not an amendment.
- The broad definition therefore very likely controls.

**Why it matters for Vaigaind:**
- The single-hall Secaucus deal becomes a portfolio-wide sole-source commitment covering every current and future North American facility of Vaigaind and its Affiliates. Under Agreement §1.1(a), "Affiliates" means more-than-50% control or common control, which may reach sister portfolio companies under a common sponsor.
- The commitment runs for the full Term. Under Issue 4, the Term could last 10+ years.
- Vaigaind loses competitive tension on pricing for every future liquid-cooling build-out.
- Vaigaind cannot honor tenant-specified or OEM-specified cooling vendors at other sites.
- The commitment could encumber acquisitions or dispositions of facilities.
- The only escape is Agreement §3.2. It applies only if *Trugeith* notifies Vaigaind that it cannot meet lead times, and only for the affected quantity.
- If Vaigaind or an Affiliate is already buying CDUs or rear-door heat exchangers from another vendor for another site, Vaigaind may already be in breach. That would be a "material breach" giving Trugeith a §15.1 termination right and a damages claim.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Amend SOW §2, ideally together with a conforming amendment to Agreement §1.1(d), so that "Covered Sites" means **the Project Site (Hall C, Secaucus) only**. At a minimum, it should mean only the specific halls in which Trugeith Products are installed under an executed SOW.
2. Delete any reference to Affiliates.
3. As a fallback:
   - limit exclusivity to Hall C replacements and expansions; or
   - convert §3.1 to a right of first offer or a "most-favored opportunity to bid" for other sites, with no purchase obligation.
4. Add an express statement that no future SOW may expand Covered Sites unless it is signed by an officer and identifies Agreement §3.1. This tracks Agreement §1.2.
5. **Ask the client** whether it, or any Affiliate, has bought or committed to buy third-party CDUs or rear-door heat exchangers since March 2, 2026 or the SOW Effective Date (August 24, 2026). Also ask what **SOW No. 1** says about Covered Sites. SOW No. 1 is not in the folder, and "the applicable SOW" is ambiguous where two SOWs exist.

---

### Issue 2: Phase 1 rejection notice was late; deemed acceptance (HIGH, time-sensitive)

**Where:**
- SOW No. 2, Recital C
- Agreement §7.3 (Rejection), also §§7.4, 7.5, 9

**Facts:**
- Agreement §7.3: Vaigaind may reject nonconforming Products by written notice "within 20 days after Delivery." If no notice is given within that period, "the Products are deemed accepted." Days are calendar days (§1.3).
- SOW Recital C: the Phase 1 CDUs were Delivered on **June 8, 2026**. The 20-day window therefore closed on **June 28, 2026**.
- Vaigaind sent its written notice of nonconformity on **July 10, 2026**, about 12 days late. The notice concerned leaking quick-disconnect couplings.
- Trugeith has rejected the notice in writing as untimely. The parties "reserve their respective positions."

**Assessment:** On the plain terms of §7.3, the July 10 notice was **not timely**. Trugeith has a strong argument that the Phase 1 CDUs were deemed accepted on June 28, 2026. The good news is that Vaigaind has not conceded the point; Recital C preserves both positions.

**Why it matters:**
- If the units were deemed accepted, Vaigaind loses the §7.4 rejection remedies. Those remedies are:
  - repair or replace within 15 days, *or a refund* of the price, at Vaigaind's option; and
  - Supplier bearing all freight, removal and reinstallation costs.
- The refund option is the most valuable leverage Vaigaind would lose.
- Leaking couplings above live IT equipment are a serious operational and tenant-liability risk. The same coupling type is being supplied in volume for Phase 2 (192 × TTS-QDC-100).

**Remedies that survive deemed acceptance:**
- **Warranty.** Agreement §7.5 provides that acceptance "does not waive Customer's rights under Section 9."
  - Under §9.1, Trugeith warrants for 36 months, from the later of Delivery and completion of commissioning, that Products conform to Specifications and are free from defects in materials, workmanship and *design*.
  - Under §9.3, Trugeith must repair or replace at its cost. If it fails to do so within a reasonable time, Vaigaind may obtain a refund. These remedies are cumulative.
- **SLS remedies.** Any coolant leak is a P1 Incident (SLS §4.1): 4-hour on-site attendance, 8-hour resolution, a permanent fix within 30 days (§4.3), and a root cause analysis (§4.4). Three P1 Incidents from the same root cause within six months are a Chronic Failure (§9.1(b)). A Chronic Failure is a material breach supporting termination (§9.3).
- **Latent-defect / revocation arguments.** Under New York law (Agreement §18.1), Vaigaind may argue that:
  - the leaks were latent and could not reasonably have been discovered within 20 days of Delivery, for example before the loop was filled, pressurized and commissioned; and
  - acceptance may be revoked where a defect substantially impairs value and was difficult to discover (NY UCC §2-608).

  How far a contractual deemed-acceptance clause limits these arguments needs further research. The answer depends on facts we do not have, including when Phase 1 was commissioned and when the leaks first appeared.

**Recommended fix:**
1. **Do not rely on the rejection remedy.** Reframe the Phase 1 claim now as a §9.1 warranty claim (defects in materials, workmanship and design), served as a formal notice under Agreement §17 with a copy to Vaigaind's General Counsel. Also log the leaks as P1 Incidents under the SLS so the response clock, root cause analysis and Chronic Failure mechanics start running.
2. **In the amendment package, negotiate a written waiver.** Trugeith would waive the §7.3 timeliness objection for the Phase 1 CDUs, or treat the July 10 notice as timely. Alternatively, it would agree a coupling remediation program: replacement of all Phase 1 quick-disconnect couplings at Trugeith's cost, under the §7.4 cost allocation. Under Agreement §19.3, any waiver must be in writing.
3. Until the issue is resolved, consider withholding disputed amounts relating to Phase 1, in good faith and with written notice under Agreement §5.3.
4. **Ask the client for:**
   - a copy of the July 10 notice and how it was delivered;
   - Trugeith's written response;
   - the Phase 1 commissioning date;
   - when, and how, the leaks were first observed; and
   - whether any earlier written communication (email, punch list, commissioning report) flagged the couplings before June 28. If so, that communication may itself qualify as a timely notice.

---

### Issue 3: DPA overrides the uncapped data-security carve-out (HIGH)

**Where:**
- DPA §8.2 (Limitation)
- Agreement §1.4 (Order of Precedence), §12.2 (Cap), §12.3(b) (Exclusions)

**What it says:**
- **Agreement §12.2** caps each party's aggregate liability at **the fees paid or payable by Customer in the 12 months preceding the event giving rise to the claim**.
- **Agreement §12.3(b)** excludes breach of Section 14 (Confidentiality and Data Security) from that cap.
- **DPA §8.2** provides: "*Notwithstanding Section 12.3(b) of the Agreement*, each Party's aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Addendum or any Security Incident … is subject to the limitation of liability in Section 12.2."
- **Agreement §1.4** ranks the **DPA first, "as to Personal Data only,"** above the Agreement body.

**Assessment:**
- Vaigaind cannot rely on Agreement §12.3(b) prevailing over the DPA. Under §1.4 the DPA controls as to Personal Data.
- DPA §8.2 expressly overrides §12.3(b).
- As a result, Trugeith's liability for a breach of its remote-monitoring platform involving Personal Data falls back under the 12-month-fees cap. That includes:
  - Vaigaind personnel data;
  - badge-access records for Hall C; and
  - tenant contact and alarm-routing data (DPA §§2.2–2.3).
- The DPA §5.5 reimbursement of notification, call-center, credit-monitoring and forensic costs is also capped.
- The phrase "relating to … any Security Incident" invites Trugeith to argue that an incident compromising both Personal Data and non-personal Customer Data is capped *in its entirety*. Non-personal Customer Data includes facility layouts and security arrangements, which Agreement §14.1 lists as Confidential Information.

**Why it matters:**
- The cap is measured by fees in the trailing 12 months, so it shrinks sharply after the capital phases are invoiced.
- Once Phase 2 Products and Services are paid, recurring fees may be mostly Remote Monitoring fees. For Phase 2 those are about 6 CDUs × $1,850 × 12 = **$133,200 per year** (SOW §7.4), plus unknown Phase 1 monitoring fees.
- A platform breach exposing tenant contacts and access records at a colocation facility could produce:
  - state breach-notification costs (NJ, NY SHIELD Act);
  - tenant claims; and
  - security-related costs.

  These could far exceed that figure.
- The clause is mutual on its face. The risk sits with Vaigaind, because Trugeith is the party processing the data.
- The override also undercuts the $10M cyber insurance Trugeith must carry (Agreement §11(e); DPA §8.3). The insurance exists, but the contract limits what Vaigaind can recover through it.

**Recommended fix:**
1. **Preferred:** delete DPA §8.2, or reverse it to state that Agreement §12.3(b) applies to liability under the DPA and for Security Incidents, so the data carve-out remains **uncapped**.
2. **Fallback:** a separate data-security **super-cap**, for example the greater of a fixed dollar amount (at least the $10M cyber limit) and a multiple of total contract fees. The DPA §5.5 response costs should sit outside or on top of it.
3. Add express language confirming that breaches of Agreement §14 involving non-personal Customer Data remain fully uncapped regardless of the DPA.
4. Conform Agreement §1.4 so that the DPA prevails only where it gives *greater* protection to Personal Data.

---

### Issue 4: Automatic five-year renewal with narrow opt-out window (MEDIUM-HIGH)

**Where:** Agreement §2.2 (Renewal); see also §§2.1, 2.3, 3.1 and SOW §9.1.

**What it says:**
- The Initial Term is five years from March 2, 2026 (§2.1).
- After that, the Agreement "shall renew automatically for successive five (5) year Renewal Terms."
- Either party may prevent renewal only by written notice delivered "during the thirty (30) day period ending two hundred seventy (270) days before the expiration of the then-current Term."
- For the Initial Term, the window is roughly **early May to about June 5, 2030**. The exact dates depend on how the March 2031 expiry date is counted and should be docketed precisely.

**Why it matters:**
- If Vaigaind misses a single 30-day window nine months before expiry, it is locked into **another five years**.
- That renewal carries with it the §3.1 exclusivity, which is portfolio-wide unless Issue 1 is fixed.
- Remote Monitoring Services also run "until the end of the Term" (SOW §9.1), so the monthly fees renew as well.
- There is no termination for convenience. The only exits are for cause (§15.1), insolvency (§15.2) or prolonged force majeure (§16).
- Under §2.3, SOWs survive expiry, which adds further tail.
- An early notice, sent before the window opens, may be ineffective. So may a late notice.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Change renewals to **one-year** Renewal Terms.
2. Allow Vaigaind to give non-renewal notice **at any time before expiry**, or on reasonable notice (for example, 60–90 days).
3. Add a Customer right to terminate for convenience during any Renewal Term.
4. Provide that exclusivity under §3.1 lapses at the end of the Initial Term regardless of renewal.
5. If the clause stays as drafted, docket the window now and send a protective notice inside it.

---

### Issue 5: Phase 2 rejection window will close before commissioning (MEDIUM)

**Where:**
- SOW §8.4, which applies Agreement §§7.1, 7.3–7.5 to the Phase 2 Products
- SOW §5.1 milestones
- Agreement §7.3

**Why it matters:**
- Phase 2 Delivery (M2) is targeted for **January 18, 2027**. The 20-day window will therefore close around **February 7, 2027**.
- Mechanical installation and pressure testing (M3) is not due until March 5, 2027.
- Commissioning (M4) is not due until April 2, 2027.
- Defects like the Phase 1 coupling leaks typically appear only under pressure and flow. The Phase 1 problem would therefore repeat on a larger scale, across 192 coupling sets and 96 rear-door heat exchangers.
- Separately, the full $4,186,400 product price is invoiced on Delivery (SOW §7.2).

**Recommended fix:**
- Amend SOW §8.4, with an Agreement §1.2-compliant reference, so that the rejection period for Phase 2 runs from the later of Delivery and **successful completion of the SOW §8.1 commissioning tests** (Substantial Completion), plus a reasonable period.
- Consider tying part of the product payment to M4.

---

### Issue 6: Secondary points (LOW)

- **Service credits are modest.** They are measured against, and capped monthly at 100% of, the Monthly Remote Monitoring Fee (SLS §§5.1, 5.4). They are expressly non-exclusive (SLS §5.6), so they do not limit damages. They are not a meaningful deterrent against a breach of the 99.99% Cooling Availability service level. Consider whether the client wants higher credits or credits tied to fees for the affected rows.
- **Freight and rigging email thread.** I found no legal issue in it. Vaigaind's consent to Hackensack Rigging & Millwright under Agreement §8.4 and SOW §10.2 is conditional on two things:
  - the crew completing the site induction before January 18, 2027; and
  - Trugeith delivering an updated certificate of insurance. Trugeith promised this by November 13, 2026.

  The project team should confirm both conditions are met before the January 18 delivery. They should also confirm the method of procedure is received by December 4, 2026. Trugeith remains responsible for the subcontractor (Agreement §8.4).

---

## 3. Recommended Approach

1. **Before January 18, 2027 (Phase 2 delivery and invoicing)**, propose a single amendment, signed by authorized officers and referencing the Agreement Sections amended (Agreement §§1.2, 19.3), that:
   - narrows Covered Sites to Hall C (Issue 1);
   - restores the uncapped data carve-out or adds a super-cap (Issue 3);
   - converts renewals to one-year terms terminable on notice (Issue 4); and
   - resets the Phase 2 rejection period to run from commissioning (Issue 5).
2. **In parallel**, serve a §9 warranty notice and log P1 Incidents for the Phase 1 couplings. Negotiate a written waiver of the §7.3 timeliness objection or a coupling replacement program (Issue 2).
3. Docket the §2.2 non-renewal window as a backstop.

---

## 4. Gaps in the Folder: Information Needed from the Client

I have not assumed answers to the following:

1. **Execution status.** All signature blocks in the folder are blank. Are the Agreement, SOW No. 2, the SLS and the DPA fully executed, and on what dates? If SOW No. 2 is unsigned, Issue 1 can be fixed simply by revising it before signature.
2. **SOW No. 1.** It is not in the folder. We need its Covered Sites definition, Phase 1 pricing, monitoring fees and commissioning terms.
3. **Phase 1 dispute file.** We need:
   - the July 10, 2026 notice and how it was delivered;
   - Trugeith's written rejection;
   - the Phase 1 commissioning report and date;
   - any earlier written communications about the couplings; and
   - the current status of the leaks.
4. **Affiliates and other sites.** We need a list of Vaigaind and Affiliate facilities in the US and Canada. We also need to know whether any third-party CDU or rear-door heat exchanger purchases or commitments are in place or planned (Issue 1 exposure).
5. **Fee profile.** Total fees paid and payable to date and forecast by year, so we can size the 12-month cap (Issue 3).
6. **Missing exhibits and notice details.**
   - Exhibit A to the SOW (Hall C Liquid Cooling Design Basis, Rev. C) is "attached separately" and not in the folder.
   - The notice-address blocks in the Agreement are blank.
7. **Insurance.** Trugeith's current certificates, including the $10M cyber policy and its terms.

Please let me know if you would like a markup of the proposed amendment or a draft of the Phase 1 warranty notice.

**MEMORANDUM**

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** Associate
**Date:** November 6, 2026
**Re:** Vaigaind Data Halls, LLC / Trugeith Thermal Systems, Inc. — Review of Hall C liquid-cooling deal documents

---

## 1. Summary

I reviewed the five documents in the folder:

- the Supply Agreement dated March 2, 2026 (the **Agreement**);
- Statement of Work No. 2 for Phase 2, Hall C (**SOW No. 2**);
- the Service Level Schedule (**SLS**);
- the Data Processing Addendum (**DPA**); and
- the Phase 2 freight and rigging email thread.

Three issues need attention. They are listed in priority order.

| # | Priority | Issue | Location |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **High (live dispute; time-sensitive)** | Phase 1 rejection notice was late, so Trugeith can claim deemed acceptance. The same mechanism threatens Phase 2. | Agreement §7.3; SOW No. 2 Recital C and §8.4 |
| 2 | **High** | The DPA overrides the Agreement's uncapped data-security carve-out and puts data and Security Incident liability back under the 12-month-fees cap. | DPA §8.2; Agreement §§1.4, 12.2, 12.3(b) |
| 3 | **Medium (long-dated, but costly if missed)** | The Agreement auto-renews for five-year terms. The only way out is a narrow 30-day non-renewal window that closes 270 days before expiry. | Agreement §2.2 |

Section 4 lists lower-priority observations. Section 5 lists the information we need from the client.

---

## 2. Priority Issues

### Issue 1 — Phase 1 rejection notice was untimely; deemed acceptance risk (HIGH)

**Where:**
- Agreement §7.3 (Rejection), §7.5 (Effect of Acceptance) and §9 (Warranties)
- SOW No. 2 Recital C and §8.4

**What the documents say:**
- Under Agreement §7.3, Vaigaind may reject nonconforming Products only by written notice of rejection within **20 days after Delivery**. If no notice is given in that period, **the Products are deemed accepted**.
- SOW No. 2 Recital C records three facts:
  - the Phase 1 CDUs were Delivered on **June 8, 2026**;
  - Vaigaind sent its written notice of nonconformity (leaking quick-disconnect couplings) on **July 10, 2026**;
  - Trugeith has rejected the notice in writing as untimely under §7.3.
- The parties "reserve their respective positions."

**Analysis:**
- The 20-day window closed on **June 28, 2026**. The July 10 notice was 12 days late.
- On the face of the documents, Trugeith has a strong argument that the Phase 1 CDUs were deemed accepted. That would cut off Vaigaind's §7.4 rejection remedies:
  - Supplier-paid repair or replacement within 15 days at Vaigaind's option, or a refund; and
  - Supplier-borne freight, removal and reinstallation costs.
- The reservation of rights in Recital C helps, because Vaigaind has not conceded the point. It does not cure the lateness.
- We should not tell the client the notice was timely.

**Why it matters:**
- Deemed acceptance moves Vaigaind from a strong rejection remedy to a narrower warranty remedy.
- Leaking couplings next to live IT equipment are a tenant-risk issue, not just a commercial one.

**Phase 2 has the same structural problem:**
- SOW No. 2 §8.4 applies Agreement §7.3 to the Phase 2 Products.
- Phase 2 Delivery (Milestone M2) is targeted for **January 18, 2027**. The 20-day window would therefore close around **February 7, 2027**.
- Commissioning, including the coupling leak inspection under design flow in SOW §8.1(b), is not targeted until **April 2, 2027** (M4).
- In other words, the rejection window will close before the tests most likely to reveal the defect Vaigaind found in Phase 1.

**Recommended fix:**

1. **Phase 1: pursue warranty remedies now.**
   - Agreement §7.5 provides that acceptance does not waive Vaigaind's rights under §9.
   - §9.1 gives a 36-month warranty, running from the later of Delivery and completion of commissioning. It covers conformity to Specifications and freedom from defects in materials, workmanship and design.
   - §9.3 requires repair or replacement at Trugeith's cost, with a refund fallback.
   - We should recast the July 10 notice, or send a supplemental notice, as a warranty claim under §9.
2. **Preserve latent-defect arguments.**
   - If the coupling leaks could not reasonably have been discovered until the units were under flow, Vaigaind has an argument for revocation of acceptance under N.Y. U.C.C. §2-608. New York law governs under Agreement §18.1.
   - That argument depends on the facts, so we need the commissioning history (see Section 5).
3. **Negotiate a written resolution.** Any waiver or extension of the §7.3 deadline must be in writing (Agreement §19.3). Options include:
   - a waiver of the Phase 1 deadline;
   - a standstill or tolling arrangement; or
   - an agreed remediation program for the Phase 1 couplings.
4. **Phase 2: change the acceptance trigger before M2.**
   - Amend the Agreement so the rejection period for Phase 2 runs from passing the commissioning tests (Substantial Completion), not from Delivery.
   - Note that SOW No. 2 §1.1 states that the SOW does not amend the Agreement. Under Agreement §1.2, an SOW can amend the Agreement only if it expressly identifies the Section amended and is signed by an authorized officer of each party.
   - This therefore needs either a properly drafted SOW amendment or a stand-alone amendment under §19.3.
5. **Interim operational step.** Ask the client to diary February 7, 2027 now. Absent an amendment, its receiving and engineering teams should send a protective, detailed §7.3 notice for any visible nonconformity well within 20 days of the January 18 delivery.

---

### Issue 2 — DPA reimposes the liability cap on data-security and Security Incident claims (HIGH)

**Where:**
- DPA §8.2
- Agreement §1.4 (Order of Precedence), §12.2 (Cap) and §12.3(b) (Exclusions)

**What the documents say:**
- **General cap.** Agreement §12.2 caps each party's aggregate liability at the **fees paid or payable by Customer under the Agreement in the 12 months preceding the event giving rise to the claim**.
- **Carve-out.** Agreement §12.3(b) excludes breach of §14 (Confidentiality and Data Security) from the cap.
- **DPA override.** DPA §8.2 provides that "**Notwithstanding Section 12.3(b) of the Agreement**," each party's aggregate liability arising out of or relating to the DPA *or any Security Incident* is subject to the §12.2 cap.
- **Precedence.** Agreement §1.4 ranks the DPA **first, as to Personal Data**, ahead of the body of the Agreement.

**Analysis:**
- Because of the precedence clause, DPA §8.2 controls for Personal Data. We should not assume the Agreement's carve-out survives.
- Trugeith processes Personal Data on its Monitoring Platform. Under DPA §§2.2 and 2.3, that data includes:
  - Vaigaind personnel data;
  - platform credentials and access logs;
  - badge-access records for Hall C and the mechanical gallery; and
  - tenant contact and alarm-routing data.
- A breach of that platform would therefore fall back under the 12-month-fees cap.
- The phrase "or any Security Incident" is broad. Trugeith will argue it also caps:
  - Vaigaind's §5.5 cost-reimbursement right (notification, call-center, credit-monitoring and forensics costs); and
  - any related §14 claim, even if it is pleaded under the Agreement.
- The clause is mutual on its face, but in practice it protects only Trugeith, because Trugeith is the processor.

**Why it matters:**
- The cap could be very small when a breach occurs. Phase 2 product and installation invoicing ends in 2027.
- After that, the recurring fees for Phase 2 are monitoring fees of $1,850 per CDU per month (SOW No. 2 §7.4). For 6 CDUs, that is about **$133,200 a year**, plus whatever Phase 1 monitoring fees apply.
- Breach-notification costs, tenant claims and regulatory exposure under the NJ Data Privacy Act and NY SHIELD Act could easily exceed that.
- The mismatch is notable because Trugeith already carries **$10 million** of cyber liability insurance (Agreement §11(e); DPA §8.3).

**Recommended fix:**

1. **Preferred:** delete DPA §8.2. Alternatively, replace it with language confirming that Agreement §12.3(b) applies to the DPA and to Security Incidents, and that DPA §5.5 costs are uncapped.
2. **Fallback:** agree a separate data super-cap set at the greater of:
   - a fixed figure aligned with the $10 million cyber policy; and
   - a multiple of annual fees.
   The super-cap should state expressly that it applies in addition to the general cap, and that §5.5 response costs and gross negligence or willful misconduct remain uncapped.
3. **Mechanics:** make the change by written amendment under DPA §10.5 and Agreement §19.3. Because of the §1.4 precedence, it is not enough to fix this in the Agreement body alone. The DPA text itself must change.

---

### Issue 3 — Five-year automatic renewal with a narrow opt-out window (MEDIUM)

**Where:**
- Agreement §2.2 (Renewal), read with §2.1 and SOW No. 2 §9.1

**What the documents say:**
- The Initial Term is five years from March 2, 2026 (Agreement §2.1).
- On expiry, the Agreement "shall renew automatically for **successive five (5) year Renewal Terms**."
- Non-renewal is effective only if notice is delivered during the **thirty (30) day period ending two hundred seventy (270) days before** expiration of the then-current Term.

**Analysis:**
- If the Initial Term expires around March 2, 2031, the window runs roughly from **early May 2030 to about June 5, 2030**.
- Notice sent before or after that window does not work on the drafting as it stands.
- The exact dates should be confirmed once we settle how "five years from the Effective Date" is computed.

**Why it matters:**
- A missed window commits Vaigaind to another full five years of the Agreement and all its terms.
- SOW No. 2 §9.1 runs the Phase 2 Remote Monitoring Services "until the end of the Term." The monitoring commitment and its fees therefore roll over with each renewal.
- The window falls about nine months before expiry, which is easy to miss in normal contract administration.

**Recommended fix:**

1. Amend §2.2 so that, after the Initial Term, the Agreement renews for **one-year terms**, terminable by Vaigaind on reasonable notice (e.g., 60–90 days) at any time before expiry.
2. Alternatively, delete automatic renewal and require mutual written agreement to renew.
3. In the interim, have the client enter the window in its contract-management system now, with reminders.
